paras: Renata Braz has read something close to four thousand company descriptions in eleven years at a mid-market fund, and she keeps two versions of the same paragraph on her desk. Both describe the same company. She calls the first one the brochure and the second one the business. “Nothing in the brochure is false,” she says. “That is the part founders never believe. It is not a lie. It is just that not one sentence in it can be checked, and a paragraph you cannot check is a paragraph nobody can pay for.”

The brochure runs like this: we serve large enterprise clients across many verticals, with a strong backlog, low churn and an experienced team. Twenty words, four claims, and no way in. “Which verticals? Strong compared to what? Experienced how? Every one of those words is fine. What is missing is the piece of the sentence that pins it to something.”

The business version is longer, and she prefers it for exactly that reason: the two verticals where we have the deepest experience are banking and logistics. Our largest client, which arrived through a referral in 2019, has renewed four times. The eleven engineers whose tenure is over five years built the platform that the incumbent supplier could not replace in two attempts. Same company. Same facts. Every claim now carries a clause that says which one, whose, or where — and every one of those clauses is something a buyer can go and verify on Monday.

The backlog line is the one she says gets rejected most often, and never because the number is low. “They quote a figure and stop. What I need is the clause: how much of it is under signed contract and how much is verbal. A founder who volunteers that distinction before I ask has just told me something about himself that no reference call would have told me.” The same goes for the footprint: not we operate across the region, but the two countries where the company has people, and the six where it only has clients.

She has one warning about the mechanism itself, which is punctuation rather than vocabulary. Our largest client, which arrived through a referral, has renewed four times and the client that arrived through a referral has renewed four times are not the same sentence. The first has one largest client and adds a detail about it; the second is identifying which client, out of several, is being talked about. “I have seen a founder bundle three products into one offer and describe it with the wrong commas, and the room spent four minutes working out whether he had one product or three. He did not lose the deal over it. But he spent four of his forty minutes on a comma, and he had planned to spend them on how they onboard a new client.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of an investor reading founder decks, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how a mid-market fund decides what a software company is worth.
To show that what makes a claim payable is the qualification attached to it -- and that in English that qualification is carried by a clause, with punctuation deciding what the clause is doing.
To argue that founders should avoid industry vocabulary in their company description.

items: She says the first version contains false statements.
She says nothing in the brochure is false. The problem is that not one sentence in it can be checked.
The largest client arrived through a referral.
It arrived through a referral in 2019 and has renewed four times.
She prefers the second paragraph because it is shorter.
It is longer, and she prefers it for exactly that reason -- every claim now carries a clause that pins it to something.
The backlog line is usually rejected because the number is too low.
Never because the number is low. It is rejected when the figure is quoted without saying how much of it is under signed contract and how much is verbal.
She says the words in the brochure are the problem.
She says every one of those words is fine. What is missing is the piece of the sentence that pins each one to something.
Moving the commas changes what the clause is doing to the sentence.
With commas there is one largest client and a detail is added; without them, the clause is identifying which client out of several is meant.

listenings.text: The founders who are easiest to work with are not the ones with the best numbers. They are the ones who qualify their own sentences before anybody asks them to. I will give you the test I use, and it takes about four minutes. I ask a very open question: tell me about your clients. A founder who is not ready says we work with large enterprises across several sectors, and then he stops and waits for the next question. A founder who is ready says our two strongest sectors are these, our largest client came to us this way and has renewed this many times, and the part of the base I actually worry about is this one. Nobody made him say the last part. He said it because he has already had the argument with himself, and once you hear that, the rest of the meeting changes. You stop testing him and you start thinking with him, which is a completely different meeting and it is the one everybody says they want.

I want to say something about long sentences, because founders get told to keep everything short and it is bad advice in this specific room. Short is right when you are pitching to a crowd. In diligence you are not pitching, you are being examined, and a short sentence in an examination is a sentence somebody else gets to finish for you. Watch what happens. You say we have a strong backlog. That is short, and now the analyst decides what strong means, and she will decide conservatively, because that is her job. Say instead: we have a backlog of this size, of which this much is under signed contract and the rest is verbal, and it sits mostly in the vertical where our delivery record is longest. That is one sentence. It is not complicated English. But there is now nothing left in it for anybody else to fill in, and the number you said is the number that goes into the model.
